query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of a controlled amount of grain-refining nanoparticles into the high-entropy alloy will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation by stabilizing grain boundaries and preventing deleterious intermetallic formation.
generation.intervention: Introduction of grain-refining nanoparticles, such as WC, which has stable chemical properties and is often used in the production of cemented carbide materials [PMC10056557::web::002::1_introduction]
generation.conditions: Service-relevant heating within the temperature range of 500°C to 800°C for a duration of 100 to 1000 hours, under loading conditions of up to 80% of the alloy's yield strength, similar to the conditions used in [PMC10708198::web::002::introduction] and [PMC11203300::web::003::1_introduction]
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and intermetallic formations, which can be stabilized by the introduction of grain-refining nanoparticles
generation.mechanism: Grain boundary stabilization and prevention of deleterious intermetallic formation, which can lead to improved toughness and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement [PMC9414008::web::001::1_introduction] and [PMC12525671::web::001::1_introduction]
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation, with a minimum of 90% retention of original toughness, while maintaining the original strength-ductility combination, similar to the properties of the Cantor alloy [PMC12525671::web::001::1_introduction]
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy exposed to the same service-relevant heating conditions, which can exhibit reduced toughness and increased brittleness [PMC10708198::web::002::introduction] and [PMC11203300::web::003::1_introduction]
generation.boundary: Temperature: 500°C to 800°C, Duration: 100 to 1000 hours, Loading: up to 80% of the alloy's yield strength, which are typical conditions for high-temperature applications [PMC11203300::web::003::1_introduction] and [PMC12430142::web::001::1_introduction]
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount and type of grain-refining nanoparticles, as well as the potential for unintended consequences such as nanoparticle agglomeration or altered corrosion resistance, which can be addressed through further research and experimentation [PMC10056557::web::002::1_introduction] and [PMC12112909::web::005::1_introduction]

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the toughness of the nanoparticle-treated alloy to the untreated baseline after exposure to service-relevant heating conditions, using techniques such as Charpy impact energy and fracture toughness testing [PMC4740901::web::014::discussion] and [PMC9848264::web::001::abstract]
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the nanoparticle-treated alloy is not significantly higher than the untreated baseline, or if the grain size and intermetallic formation are not significantly improved, the hypothesis is falsified

As a kind of comprehensive material, high entropy alloy has better physical and chemical properties than many common metal compounds []. Therefore, it has attracted wide attention in material science and engineering and is the focus field of scholars at home and abroad [,]. In recent years, many scholars at home and abroad have used high entropy alloys for surface modification, mainly by laser melting, laser deposition, and plasma melting. The lower preparation cost and excellent performance of high entropy alloys not only improve their service life and significantly reduce the failure loss but also reduce their surface repair cost, and high entropy alloys have many advantages that traditional alloys can hardly match []. However, there are difficulties in the synergistic enhancement of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance of high entropy alloys, and no satisfactory solution has been found so far []. The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). Recent studies have revealed that refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements such as tungsten (W), molybdenum (Mo), niobium (Nb), and tantalum (Ta) exhibit superior high-temperature strength and good fatigue resistance, surpassing the currently used nickel-based superalloys [,]. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as critical materials in industrial applications. As the aerospace, energy, automotive, and defense industries continue to evolve, the demand for advanced alloy materials has grown significantly []. HEAs exhibit outstanding high-temperature strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance, making them ideal candidates for extreme environments such as aircraft engines, gas turbines, chemical reactors, and nuclear facilities [,,,,]. The NiAlNbTiV HEA demonstrates superior hardness, exceptionally high-temperature performance, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and relative stability [,,], while exposure of the NiAlNbTiV HEA to high-temperature and high-pressure conditions results in significant surface wear, which degrades its mechanical properties and indirectly raises operational costs [,,].

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) constitute one of the most innovative classes of metallic materials, attracting significant attention from both scientific and industrial communities in recent years [,,]. Their uniqueness lies in the design of chemical composition, where several principal elements are present in nearly equimolar proportions, leading to the formation of high-entropy phases with simplified crystalline structures [,]. These materials exhibit exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties, often surpassing those of traditional engineering alloys [,]. HEAs, particularly the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi), remain among the most recognized and extensively studied representatives within this group []. Since its discovery, the Cantor alloy has attracted significant scientific attention due to its exceptional mechanical properties, distinguishing it from both conventional and other HEAs [,]. It exhibits a single-phase FCC structure with excellent ductility and resistance to brittle fracture, even under cryogenic conditions [,,]. The concept of high entropy alloy (HEA) was proposed and published in 2004 [,,] and the unique properties of these alloys have attracted attention from research groups all over the world. The pioneering studies by Cantor et al. were the first to report that an equiatomic alloy consisting of the five transition metals Cr, Mn, Fe, Co and Ni crystallized as a single solid solution [,] in the as-cast and in the homogenized state. The first HEA generation could contain five or more main elements with the concentration of each element in the range 5–35 at. % []. The alloys presented a high mixing entropy in their liquid state [] and thus could form simple solid solution structures (e.g., FCC, BCC and HCP) in place of intermetallic phases. Some promising technological characteristics of HEAs were high hardness [], good wear resistance [], excellent strength at both high and low temperatures [,,] and generally a good resistance to oxidation and corrosion [].
